subject: Deciding on bin numbers and truncation

messages.author: e53c8e38b16419a5
messages.subject: Deciding on bin numbers and truncation
parts:
Hello,

 

I am a new Distance user (using Distance 6.2), and I have a question about binning and truncating data. With various combinations of bin numbers and truncation, I get slightly different results for Density and CV. Without binning and truncation I get the warning “Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity.” With binning and truncation, the curve gets better and no warnings appear (green light on the Results tab). My question is: How do I decide which analysis is more reliable? I feel like using the analysis with no errors and the lowest CV would be best. Is that right? Am I on the right track?

 

I appreciate any help with this,

 

Brigham Whitman

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Deciding on bin numbers and truncation
parts:
Brigham

A couple of comments: warning are not the same as errors.  The warning is suggesting there is a "spike" in your data at distance > 0.  That's not inherently wrong; you need simply to understand why that hump in your data exists.

Using a small CV is a *bad* idea for model selection; it may lead to confidence intervals that are too narrow to include the true parameter.

General rule: use exact distances if possible, they provide more information about the fit of your model to your data.  Bin if there is rounding to preferred distances (better yet, don't round to preferred distances when collecting data).

When noting differences in density estimates from different analyses, place those differences in the context of the precision of the estimates themselves.  A 5% difference between analyses is small if the CVs are 30%.
